In line with his overall approach, the Chronicler idealizes Solomon. By bringing out his strengths and omitting his failures, he presents Solomon as a role model for his own contemporaries and also heightens their anticipation of the coming one who will completely fulfill what is required of Him.

**1:1–17** This section is balanced by a concluding section dealing with Solomon’s wisdom and wealth (9:13–28). Here, however, worship also plays a significant role, a feature sadly lacking in the closing account.

**1:1 established himself.** The Chronicler frequently uses such expressions to indicate success after difficulty (12:13; 13:21; 17:1; 25:11; 27:6). Indirectly, he acknowledges that Solomon’s rise to power has been tumultuous, although he omits the details given in 1 Kin. 2 (1 Chr. 23:1 note).

**God was with him.** Solomon’s success is the result of God’s sovereign blessing in fulfillment of David’s hopes (1 Chr. 22:11, 16; 28:20).

This passage roughly follows 1 Kin. 3:4–15, but the account is expanded somewhat, emphasizing the theme of Solomon’s reign over “all Israel” (v. 2; see 1 Chr. 11:1) and explaining why Solomon went to Gibeon, eight miles (13 km) northwest of Jerusalem, to sacrifice (vv. 3–6).

In the course of building the temple, Solomon emerges as a kind of counterpart to Bezalel, who helped construct the tabernacle (see 2:14). See notes on 1 Chr. 2:20 and Ex. 31:1–11.

**sought it out.** The Hebrew is ambiguous. Rather than referring to the altar, it may mean “sought Him out” (see text note), a reference to the Lord, which is the noun nearest to the unspecified pronoun.

The splendor and power of Solomon’s reign is the result of divinely bestowed wisdom, a term implying discernment and capacity for effective action. In his wisdom, Solomon foreshadows Christ, who is the wisdom of God incarnate (Is. 11:1, 2; Col. 2:3).

**knowledge.** This also contains a practical component. It is not merely possession of facts but the ability to use them to inform suitable conduct.

The account in Kings ends with Solomon’s sacrifice in Jerusalem (1 Kin. 3:15). Passing over this as well as Solomon’s judgment between the two mothers (1 Kin. 3:16–28), Chronicles focuses on Solomon’s temple construction as a demonstration of his wisdom.

Trading in horses and chariots is an aspect of international arms dealings in Solomon’s time.

In this section the Chronicler makes use of 1 Kin. 12–2 Kin. 17, but about half his materi­al comes from other sources. His record of the period of the divided monarchy does not rehearse the harsh condemnation of the northern tribes found in Kings, focusing instead on events in Judah, the location of the temple, and the Davidic king. Throughout this section, the writer reports how the conditions in the kingdom depend on the king’s faithfulness to God and the guidance he gives to the nation. As the original readers considered these events, they could see clearly the choices for blessing and curse in their own day.

**10:1–12:16** In describing Rehoboam’s reign (931–913 B.C.), the Chronicler makes broad use of Kings (cf. 10:1–11:4 with 1 Kin. 12:1–24; 12:9–16 with 1 Kin. 14:21, 25–31) while presenting the material in accord with his own theological understanding and emphasis. The account is presented in two parts (10:1–11:23 and 12:1–14), each narrating a problematic situation, prophetic encounter, and divine blessing. The conclusion is a notice of Rehoboam’s wars with Jeroboam and his death (12:15, 16). The chapters impress on the readers God’s curse against pride and infidelity and the benefits of living in humility and obedience to the prophetic word (20:20 note).

**10:1–11:23** The first section recounting Rehoboam’s reign focuses on the initial three years of his rule (11:17), in which there is conflict (ch. 10), obedience to the prophetic word (11:1–4), and divine blessing (11:5–23). 10:1–11:4 is derived from 1 Kin. 12:1–24 (notes); the Chronicler adds 11:5–23.

The last usage is found here. The gathering of all the tribes is for recognition of his kingship.

This appointment is typical of the co-regencies (overlapping reigns between father and son) that prevail in Judah and provide a clear line of succession there.

By dispersing his sons throughout Judah and settling them there rather than keeping them at court, Rehoboam tries to forestall plotting against his chosen heir and also strengthens royal control of the land.

For the second major portion of the account of Rehoboam’s reign (10:1–12:16 note), the historian expands the account of 1 Kin. 14:25–28. He reports Rehoboam’s disobedience in his fourth year and divine retribution by means of Shishak’s invasion in his fifth year (12:2).

**12:1, 2 abandoned the law ... unfaithful to the** LORD**.** Three years that witnessed consolidation of Rehoboam’s rule in the south are followed by a fourth in which the king and nation fall prey to pride and self-reliance. See 1 Kin. 14:22–24 for more details on their apostasy involving adoption of Canaanite idolatry and associated immoral practices. See also note on 1 Chr. 16:40.

**12:1 all Israel.** The southern kingdom alone as embodying the covenant community. See note on 10:1.

**12:2 unfaithful.** They violate the terms of the covenant, particularly regarding worship of the Lord. See note on 1 Chr. 2:7.

**Shishak.** Most scholars identify him as Sheshonk I, founder of the Twenty-Second Dynasty of Egypt (c. 945–924 B.C..), whose military campaign extended north to the plains of Jezreel and Megiddo.

The author adds these verses to complete the parallel with Rehoboam’s previous encounter with Shemaiah (cf. 11:2–4; 10:1–11:23 note).

**12:3 1,200 ... 60,000 ... without number.** See note on 1 Chr. 19:7. “Sukkiim” are Libyan mercenary forces, who are mentioned in Egyptian texts.
Rehoboam’s newly strengthened fortress towns (11:5–12) prove incapable of resisting the might of Egypt.
First appears in 11:2; here he tells the leaders of Judah that they have brought this attack on themselves by their religious compromise (see 1 Chr. 28:9; 2 Chr. 15:2).
See also vv. 7, 12. This event illustrates God’s response to Solomon’s prayer (7:14 note). It remains a standing principle of devout conduct (1 Pet. 5:6).

Although Shemaiah modifies his first warning, God’s sovereign plan is not overturned. Prophetic warnings are designed to stir repentance. If successful, the threat of judgment is often removed, postponed, or softened (Jer. 18:1–12; Joel 2:12–14; Jon. 3)., 8
The glory of Solomon’s kingdom has already faded, and the people are forced into surrendering its trappings, which are taken as plunder to Egypt.
The key lesson the Chronicler wants to impress on his audience is that while Rehoboam continues to suffer for his sins, God graciously establishes his kingdom and blesses the nation.
Probably a reference to the sins of Rehoboam’s fourth year (vv. 1, 2 note). This observation is not found in 1 Kin. 14:29–31.
See Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Literary Features. Some of the additional sources from which the Chronicler derives his information.

The account of Abijah’s reign in Chronicles (13:2–21) differs considerably from that in Kings (1 Kin. 15:3–5). Chronicles emphasizes the positive side of Abijah’s reign, while the writer of Kings focuses on the negative side (1 Kin. 15:3). The Chronicler reports Abijah’s speech against the northern kingdom (13:4–12) and his prayerful reliance on God in battle (13:14).

**13:1 Abijah.** He reigned 913–910 B.C.., during the rule of Jeroboam I in the northern kingdom (930–909 B.C.). His name is spelled Abijam in 1 Kin. 15:1–8.

A variant spelling of “Maacah” (see 11:20; 1 Kin. 15:2). Maacah is apparently the granddaughter of Absalom through his daughter Tamar and her husband, Uriel of Gibeah.

**war between Abijah and Jeroboam.** 1 Kin. 15:6, 7 mentions this war, but Chronicles has more details, including the drawing of battle lines, Abijah’s speech, the battle itself, and its outcome.

Judah is greatly outnumbered, highlighting the power of God at work on behalf of faithful Judah (1 Chr. 12:23 note; 1 Chr. 19:7 note). The seemingly high numbers are in line with those recorded in 1 Chr. 21:5.

Abijah’s speech against the northern kingdom makes clear that David’s dynasty is approved by God and that the temple worship in Jerusalem is established by God.

**13:4 Mount Zemaraim.** In the border regions between Judah and Israel, probably in the territory of Benjamin (see Josh. 18:22).

The revelation embodied in the covenant and its institutions create additional obligations upon those who are aware of it. The rebellion of the north is still a recent event, and those addressed by Abijah should not suppress the truth they learned earlier.

**a covenant of salt.** Probably symbolic of the permanence of the covenant because of salt’s preservative qualities (Lev. 2:13; Num. 18:19).
Abijah appeals to the northern army by blaming Jeroboam for the rebellion against Rehoboam.

verse_quote: young and irresolute and could not withstand them.
note: Abijah explains that Rehoboam’s offense against the northern tribes (10:1–17) is the result of his youth (in fact, he is forty-one years old) and inexperience (see 1 Chr. 22:5; 29:1; 2 Chr. 12:13).

LORD**.** Despite Rehoboam’s offense, to oppose David’s dynasty was to resist God Himself. “Withstand” is literally “to strengthen oneself before,” but it was a false confidence despite the larger army of the north.

In contrast to the northern kingdom, Judah has remained fundamentally loyal to the temple, priests, and Levites (but see 12:1, 2). As Hezekiah’s later reforms indicate, Judah’s faithfulness does not endure (29:4–11 note; 30:6–9 note).

Abijah’s speech refers to his care for proper worship, and is an important message for the original readers of Chronicles during their reestablishment of worship in Jerusalem after the exile.

**13:12 God is with us.** See Num. 14:9; Ps. 46:7; notes on Is. 7:14; Matt. 1:23. Abijah asserts that God is with Judah, even in a fight against the northern kingdom. The northern kingdom’s conduct is perverse and doomed to fail, but the presence of God with the army of Judah will secure victory.
LORD**.** In his dedicatory prayer, Solomon spoke of praying to God in battle (6:34 note). Prayer appears here as the decisive factor in the battle (1 Chr. 4:9 note).
In this context, the northern kingdom.

See note on 1 Chr. 20:4. This is the same verb as “to humble oneself” (see 7:14). Those who do not voluntarily humble themselves before God will be made to bow.

**because they relied on the** LORD**.** Reliance on the power of the Lord instead of on human strength is a dominant theme in Chronicles (16:2 note).

The outcomes for Jeroboam and Abijah indicate whether God approves or disapproves of them. Jeroboam never recovers from his defeat. Abijah, however, grows stronger and has many children (1 Chr. 13:13 note)., 21

note: Iddo was mentioned in 9:29, and his “story” or “record” is another source used by the Chronicler. See Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Literary Features.

This account of Asa’s reign is considerably longer than that of 1 Kin. 15:9–24 (forty-eight verses as compared to sixteen). Asa’s reign is presented in two parts: years of fidelity and blessing (14:1–15:19) and later years of infidelity and curse (ch. 16). Within these two parts there is a pattern of contrasting parallels: Asa’s growing prosperity (14:1–7) is balanced by the concluding section on his illness and death (16:11–14). This change of circumstances is explained in the central section where Asa is first presented as reliant on God and successful in war (14:9–15). This is followed by words of prophetic commendation and royal reform (ch. 15). By way of contrast, in his later years Asa relies on human power and allies himself with a foreign king (16:1–6) and so incurs prophetic condemnation (16:7–9), to which he reacts harshly (16:10). Again the Chronicler is drawing on the past to make the options more vivid for his own and succeeding generations.

**14:1** A transitional verse, moving from the reign of Abijah to that of Asa.

**the land had rest.** See note on 1 Chr. 22:9. Asa has a lengthy reign, from 911 to 870/869 B.C. In his first ten years, his reforming zeal is blessed with national security (911–900 B.C.).

Asa removes pagan high places (see 1 Kin. 3:2 note) from both Jerusalem and “all the cities of Judah” (14:5), but 15:17 (1 Kin. 15:14) indicates that he does not continue his initial efforts throughout his life. A similar explanation holds for the descriptions of Jehoshaphat’s removal of high places (see 17:6; 20:33).

LORD**.** See note on 7:14.

**keep the law and the commandment.** See note on 1 Chr. 16:40.

It is later noted that “the high places were not taken out of Israel [= Judah]” (15:17; 1 Kin. 15:14). Possibly the emphasis here should be on “the cities of Judah” with high places in the countryside remaining. More probably Asa’s early reforms have only a superficial impact on the people, and later in his reign there is a resurgence of Canaanite practices.

Apparently this means that there are no major wars in this period. The writer says later that Asa captures some towns in Ephraim during this time (15:8).

**the LORD gave him peace.** Chronicles presents peace in Asa’s reign as a blessing for devotion and obedience to God (14:2–16:14 note; 1 Chr. 22:9 note).

**14:6, 7 He built ... Let us build.** God also assists Asa’s building projects (1 Chr. 11:5 note).

**14:7 because we have sought the** LORD**.** Asa plainly says that his success comes from having sought God (v. 4). This is not uttered complacently. Past faithfulness has been rewarded and has become the basis for further faithful action—just the message for the Chronicler’s generation.

When Zerah attacks, Asa seeks the Lord and gains victory, fulfilling Solomon’s request in his prayer (6:34 note). This battle directly contrasts with Asa’s later battle against Baasha (16:1–6; see 14:2–16:14 note).

**14:8** Asa’s army totals 580,000. The attacking army is nearly twice as large (“a million men,” v. 9). On these large numbers, see note on 1 Chr. 12:23.

Possibly a general of Pharaoh Osorkon I, second ruler of the Twenty-Second Dynasty of Egypt. Ethiopia (or Cush) in the Bible is the remote region south of Egypt, corresponding to modern-day northern Sudan (1 Chr. 1:8). This invasion seems to occur shortly before Asa’s fifteenth year (see 15:10).

**a million men.** See note on 1 Chr. 19:7.

**Mareshah.** About twenty-five miles (40 km) southwest of Jerusalem.

Asa expresses his utter inadequacy for battle against Zerah (20:12 note).

**we rely on you.** Reliance on the Lord’s power is the key to Asa’s victory (16:7 note).
A Philistine city that lies twenty miles (32 km) southwest of Mareshah. The area around Gerar seems already to be under Egyptian control.

As the army returns from Gezer (see v. 11), Azariah proclaims the principle of retribution so often illustrated in this account of the divided monarchy. Faithfulness to God will bring blessing; disloyalty will result in chastisement.
See notes on 7:14 and 1 Chr. 28:9.

That is, without His presence and blessing. “Without a teaching priest” implies they are neglecting their duties in this respect (Lev. 10:11), so there is no true knowledge of the law or obedience to it. Probably a reference to the days of the judges so that “Israel” is the whole nation.
LORD**.** See note on 7:14.

Asa responds to the prophet with further reforms (v. 8) and an assembly of covenant renewal (vv. 9–15); he goes so far as to depose Maacah, his relative, because of her religious apostasy (vv. 16–19).

**15:8 repaired the altar of the** LORD**.** The great bronze altar in the outer courtyard. Exactly how it was damaged is not known.
Israelites from the northern tribes (11:14 note) defect and join Asa as he suppresses idolatry and reestablishes true worship in Jerusalem.

verse_quote: the third month of the fifteenth year.
note: Probably coincides with the celebration of the Feast of Weeks/Pentecost in May/June 895 B.C.

A renewed pledge of adherence to the Sinai covenant as a seal of their wholehearted participation in their special relationship with the Lord. Significant for the Chronicler is that Asa (15:12), Jehoiada (23:16), Hezekiah (29:10), and Josiah (34:30–32) all lead the nation in such renewals, celebrating God’s goodness to His people over the generations. In this way, the author emphasizes to his contemporaries the importance of adhering to their similar commitments (Ezra 10:3–5; Neh. 9:38).
The law of Moses prescribes capital punishment for those who seek other gods (Ex. 22:20; Deut. 13:6–16).
See note on 1 Chr. 22:9.

His grandmother has the same name (11:20), so “mother” may be used in an extended sense. In either case, Asa does not let family connections compromise his loyalty to the Lord.

**at the brook Kidron.** Outside Jerusalem, to the east.
See note on 14:3.

See note on 14:6.

**15:19–16:1 thirty-fifth year ... thirty-sixth year.** Kings reports that Elah succeeded Baasha in Asa’s twenty-sixth year (1 Kin. 15:33; 16:8), Zimri in Asa’s twenty-seventh year (1 Kin. 16:10, 15), and Omri in Asa’s thirty-first year (1 Kin. 16:23). Consequently, this battle could not have taken place in the thirty-sixth year of Asa (16:1) since Baasha would have been dead for ten years. No simple solution to this difficulty has been found. One suggestion is that an original “twenty-fifth” and “twenty-sixth” was inadvertently changed through a copyist’s error (see Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Special Issues). A plausible alternative is that the Chronicler’s source here used a chronology dating from the division of the kingdom, so that the thirty-fifth and thirty-sixth years of the kingdom correspond to what is elsewhere be expressed as Asa’s fifteenth and sixteenth years, respectively. Understood in this way, it eliminates the problem of Baasha’s waiting for ten years until 885/884 B.C. before trying to stem the flow of his subjects to the south, which began in 895 B.C.

Asa’s battle with Baasha of Israel begins his downfall. He seeks the assistance of Ben-hadad of Syria, in sharp contrast with his battle against Zerah when he relied on the Lord (14:2–16:14 note).

**16:1 Ramah.** On the border between the two kingdoms, five miles (8 km) north of Jerusalem. Baasha is trying to prevent further defections to the south.

verse_quote: treasures of the house of the LORD ... to Ben-hadad.
note: Asa’s actions are wrong on two counts. First, he takes from the temple treasuries, showing disregard for the temple and its worship (see 28:21). Second, he allies himself with a foreign power instead of relying on the Lord. He compounds this fault in that the foreign alliance is against northern Israel. The Chronicler demonstrates many times the benefits of relying on God (1 Chr. 5:20; 2 Chr. 13:18; 14:11–15; 16:7, 8; 32:20–22). He also deplores foreign alliances and points to their dire consequences (18:1; 19:2; 20:35–37; 22:3–9; 25:7; 28:16–21; 35:21 note), a suitable warning to those engaged in rebuilding the nation after the return from exile in Babylon.

verse_quote: a covenant between me and you.
note: An international treaty, here one between equals. Asa’s payment is not tribute but a bribe to induce Ben-hadad to repudiate his alliance with Israel. Making this covenant is a sad reversal of the scene found in 15:12.

–**6** Ben-hadad captures several cities in the far north of Israel, and this diverts Baasha’s attention from his southern border. Asa is therefore able to take over the newly constructed border post at Ramah, reusing its building materials on other sites nearby. The record is one of success for Asa’s political strategy.

In contrast to the earlier episode of Azariah’s encouragement and Asa’s reforms (ch. 15), Hanani is sent to deliver a prophetic rebuke to King Asa, who reacts negatively (14:2–16:14 note). This is the first recorded persecution of a prophet.

**16:7 you relied.** This verb occurs three times in vv. 7, 8 (elsewhere in Chronicles only in 13:18; 14:11). It points to seeking God’s assistance in a time of national crisis. Even though a measure of military success is achieved, the whole enterprise is flawed because it is not based on faith in God and what He will achieve for His people.

**escaped you.** Baasha deserts his position before the arrival of Asa and Ben-hadad, cutting short Asa’s victory (16:5).
Hanani refers directly to the contrast with Asa’s victory over Zerah (14:8–15). “Ethiopians” means people from south of Egypt (see 14:9 note). The Libyans are from North Africa, west of Egypt.

verse_quote: from now on you will have wars.
note: Hanani threatens divine judgment because of Asa’s infidelity (1 Chr. 28:9 note; 2 Chr. 14:6 note).
Presumably those who agree with Hanani the prophet.

verse_quote: the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel
note: . Not the canonical books of Kings but an earlier court chronicle.

Asa’s rejection of the prophetic word leads to his disease and death (14:2–16:14 note).

**thirty-ninth year.** 872/871 B.C., two years before his death in 870/869 B.C.

**physicians.** Asa continues to turn away from the Lord and rely on human strength. The OT does not hesitate to prescribe medical treatment for physical maladies (2 Kin. 20:5–7 and the use of balm in Jer. 8:22; 51:8), but it never divorces natural remedies from seeking divine assistance (Deut. 32:39).

verse_quote: made a very great fire in his honor.
note: These fires are not cremations but memorials honoring deceased kings. Cf. the honor bestowed on Asa with the response to Jehoram’s death (21:19).

The account of Jehoshaphat’s reign incorporates most of the record in Kings (cf. 1 Kin. 22:1–35 with 2 Chr. 18:2–34; 1 Kin. 22:41–46, 49 with 2 Chr. 20:31–36) but is twice as long, adding some material and a summary of his reign. The Chronicler views Jehoshaphat positively in general. In his earlier reign, Jehoshaphat is faithful (17:3–9) and faces battle (18:1–19:3). Later he again is faithful (19:4–11) and again faces battle (20:1–30). The Chronicler once more brings out the need to respond properly to God’s Word (18:4–27; 20:14–21) and the power of effective prayer (18:31; 20:5–17). Also, foreign alliances are to be avoided as they substitute reliance on human scheming and power for faithful trust in the Lord. Jehoshaphat is portrayed as a man of faith who is somewhat naive (18:29) and whose otherwise creditable desire to promote good relations with the north and a changed religious outlook there leads him to make several unwise moves.

**17:1 Jehoshaphat.** He reigned 873–848 B.C. Jehoshaphat was probably co-regent with Asa for three years (873–870/869 B.C.) because of Asa’s illness (16:11–14; see 20:31 note). At the beginning of his reign, there continued to be hostility toward the northern kingdom, which was by that time ruled by Ahab.
See note on 14:6.

The Chronicler hints that David’s later ways (2 Sam. 11–21) were different.

**the Baals.** This reflects the Baal worship of Canaan and Phoenicia, which is being promoted at this time in Israel by Ahab and his wife, Jezebel (1 Kin. 16:31).
See note on 14:3. Just as in the reign of his father, Asa (14:5; 15:17), the king’s initial removal of these sites of pagan worship is later reversed due to popular attachment to them (see 20:33).

This teaching mission probably takes place just after Asa’s death (17:1 note).

**17:7, 8 officials ... Levites.** The royal officials are accompanied by Levites, whom Moses ordained to be teachers of the people (1 Chr. 26:29–32 note; 2 Chr. 19:5–11 note).

verse_quote: the Book of the Law of the
note: LORD**.** The identity of this book is uncertain. It may include the entire Pentateuch, but in light of the nature of Jehoshaphat’s reforms (19:4–11), it certainly includes Deuteronomy.
LORD**.** Fear of the divine power displayed in Jehoshaphat’s military strength gives him peace with other nations (1 Chr. 14:17 note). Some indeed pay him tribute (v. 11).
See note on 1 Chr. 11:5.
For these large numbers, see note on 1 Chr. 12:23.

In contrast to his early years, Jehoshaphat comes under God’s curse because he ignores the prophetic warning and makes an alliance with the northern kingdom (16:2 note; 20:20 note).

**18:1 he made a marriage alliance.** The author refers to the marriage of Jehoshaphat’s son Jehoram to Athaliah, daughter of Ahab (21:6; 22:2). In Kings, Ahab (874–853 B.C.) represents the depths of apostasy in the northern kingdom (1 Kin. 16:30). See note on 16:2; 19:1–3.

Probably near the end of Ahab’s reign.

**induced.** The Hebrew expression can have the connotation of enticing to apostasy (Deut. 13:6; 1 Chr. 21:1).

**Ramoth-gilead.** A city thirty miles (48 km) east of the Jordan River, closer to the Sea of Galilee than the Dead Sea. Moses set it apart as a city of refuge in Israel (Deut. 4:43; Josh. 20:8), but it was captured later by the father of Ben-hadad, the king of Syria against whom Ahab fought several battles. Ben-hadad eventually agreed to return the city to Israel, but he failed to do so (1 Kin. 20:1–34).
Jehoshaphat tries to still his conscience and regain some initiative in the situation by requiring the Lord’s approval for the proposed enterprise.

Jehoshaphat perceives that though the prophets are presenting themselves as prophets of the Lord (see “another”), they are not speaking by divine direction. He therefore asks for a genuine prophet to inquire of the Lord’s will.
Zedekiah’s enacted prophecy may be an attempt to invoke the Mosaic blessing of the Joseph tribes in Deut. 33:17.
An attempt to coerce Micaiah to fall in with the majority viewpoint and say what the king wants to hear, but Micaiah rejects such compromise (v. 13).
The mocking, ironic tone of Micaiah’s response is evident to Ahab.
LORD**.** Micaiah’s vision of heavenly deliberations (see Job 1:6–12; Is. 6:1–8; Zech. 3) demonstrates that the sovereignty of God extends over evil events (1 Chr. 21:1 note).
A singular form, referring to Ahab.
The designation of a court official who enforces royal orders rather than a member of Ahab’s family (see Jer. 36:26; 38:6).

In contrast to Rehoboam (11:4) and Asa after his first battle (15:1–8), Jehoshaphat pays no attention to the prophet’s warning. As a result, Jehoshaphat barely escapes with his life (18:31). See note on 20:20.
Ahab tries to make Jehoshaphat a target for the enemy, and, unsuspectingly, Jehoshaphat does not see the danger he is in.

The writer adds to the words of 1 Kings 22:32 the explicit statement that “the LORD helped him,” recalling the request of Solomon’s dedicatory prayer (6:34 note; 7:14 note). Even though Jehoshaphat is engaged in an enterprise that the Lord has not sanctioned, when he cries out in prayer, he receives divine assistance.
The writer does not repeat the details of Ahab’s death found in 1 Kin. 22:36–40.

Jehoshaphat escapes death after crying out to the Lord (18:31). Even so, Jehu rebukes him for his sin. God earlier chastised Jehoshaphat for depending on a foreign alliance (16:7–10 note; 1 Chr. 28:9 note).
LORD**.** This does not interdict compassion for the lost (Matt. 5:44) but does forbid compromise with God’s enemies and involvement in their schemes (Ps. 139:21, 22).

verse_quote: some good is found in you.
note: Jehoshaphat is guilty of inconsistency, but despite that, the Lord will bless him.
Jehoshaphat personally travels throughout the kingdom from Beersheba in the south to the northern border with Israel to draw the people back to allegiance to God.
Jehoshaphat establishes a system of courts throughout Judah to enforce the Mosaic law (1 Chr. 26:20–32). He earlier sent out leaders, Levites, and priests to teach (17:7–9).
This does not mean that their decisions are inspired but that God approves of the work of the courts in general and wants their decisions to be made according to His law.

Jehoshaphat also sets up a supreme court in Jerusalem to hear appeals. The king’s arrangements provide for religious cases to be heard by the chief priest and civil cases by a royal administrator. Zebadiah is not the same individual as the Levite of that name in 17:8. Details of such judicial arrangements were of interest to the Chronicler’s postexilic readers because the Persians granted them the right to organize local courts.

This battle is not found in Kings. Jehoshaphat responds to a serious military threat with exemplary reliance on the Lord (cf. his approach to the battle in 18:1–19:3). This incident probably occurs shortly after the defeat at Ramoth-gilead.

**20:1 Moabites ... Ammonites.** The descendants of these enemies are still a threat to Israel after the return from exile in Babylon (Neh. 2:19; 4:1–3; 13).

**Meunites.** Members of an Arabian tribe who live south and east of the Dead Sea, including in the territory of Edom (1 Chr. 4:41; 2 Chr. 26:7). Possibly at this time they are dwelling in Mount Seir (v. 10), probably located in the south of Edom.

See note on 1 Chr. 19:7.

**Edom.** Although virtually all Hebrew manuscripts read “Aram,” that is, Syria (text note), there is no mention of Aram in the context. The Hebrew for Edom and Aram differ only in one letter, so there may have been a tendency for copyists to accidentally misread “Edom” as “Aram.” See Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Special Issues.

**Engedi.** On the west shore of the Dead Sea, en route to Jerusalem.
Jehoshaphat responds immediately by calling Judah to fast and seek the Lord; these actions recall Solomon’s dedicatory prayer (6:34 notes).

**believe his prophets, and you will succeed.** 2 Chronicles frequently emphasizes the importance of trusting and obeying the prophetic word. See notes on chs. 10–12; 14:2–16:14; 18:1–19:3; 24:19; 25:1–13; 25:15, 16; 28:5–15; 36:15 (see also Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Characteristics and Primary Themes). Jehoshaphat’s instruction contrasts with his earlier rejection of Micaiah (18:1–32).
See note on 5:13.

See note on 14:3.

The Chronicler supplements the record of Jehoram’s reign in Kings (2 Kin. 8:16–24); in Kings, the assessment is negative. Jehoram reigned as co-regent with Jehoshaphat from 853 to 848 B.C. (2 Kin. 1:17; 3:1) and by himself from 848 to 841 B.C.. As sole monarch (21:1–20 note).

verse_quote: not willing to destroy the house of David.

The reign of Hezekiah (c. 727–c. 696 B.C.; cf. 2 Kin. 18:1, 2; 21:1 notes; Is. 36:1 note) begins a new era in the history of Israel and Judah. The northern kingdom has been destroyed by the Assyrians, and only Judah remains. Hezekiah is portrayed as bringing together representatives from both kingdoms so as to form a single, reunited kingdom with one king and one temple in Jerusalem.

**29:1 Hezekiah.** The Chronicler devotes more attention to Hezekiah than to any other king except David and Solomon. He uses material from 2 Kin. 18–20, but he supplements it extensively with other details, including an lengthy account of Hez­ekiah’s temple reforms and Passover celebration (29:3–31:1). Hezekiah’s reign appears as a return to the glory of Solomon’s kingdom. In particular, Hezekiah’s Passover reunites the separated kingdoms under a Davidic king. This anticipates the future that the Chronicler believes awaits the restored people in postexilic Israel.

The Chronicler’s assessment of Hezekiah is totally positive, and he passes quickly over Hezekiah’s failings as not relevant to the lessons from history he is trying to teach. Although David is mentioned here, the Chronicler repeatedly compares Hezekiah to Solomon.
